articles.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
articles.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.
articles.content:
A new Stanford Medicine-led study has identified three distinct biological brain types, known as biotypes, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety disorder or both conditions.

The findings could help unravel the complicated relationship between two of the most common childhood mental health disorders, which frequently share symptoms. Published recently in Nature Mental Health, the study reveals that each biotype involves disruptions in a different set of brain circuits.

By examining thousands of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three biological patterns associated with different groups of symptoms. These findings could eventually help doctors recognize ADHD and anxiety earlier, identify new targets for treatment, and determine which therapies are most likely to benefit individual patients.

"The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses," said co-senior study author Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences.

Doctors currently rely on symptom checklists to diagnose ADHD and anxiety. However, Zhang explained that children diagnosed with either disorder frequently experience symptoms associated with the other.

Looking Beyond Traditional ADHD and Anxiety Diagnoses

Yong Jiao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Iowa, is the study's lead author. Zhang shares senior authorship with Jing Jiang, PhD, assistant professor of pediatric neurology at the University of Iowa.

"We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic," Zhang said.

The researchers found that the relationship was not so straightforward. Children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety or both could belong to any of the three brain biotypes, although some biological patterns were more prevalent among children with particular diagnoses.

According to the researchers, identifying these underlying differences could add a valuable layer of biological information to existing diagnostic categories, benefiting both future research and clinical care.

AI Uncovers Hidden Patterns in Thousands of Brain Scans

The research team drew on data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, an ongoing investigation of brain development involving more than 11,000 children across the United States. Participants were 9 or 10 years old when they entered the project.

The analysis included 3,508 children who already had a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both when they enrolled, along with 693 children who initially had neither diagnosis but subsequently developed one or both conditions. Another 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis served as a control group.

All participants underwent fMRI brain scans and completed a series of cognitive and behavioral assessments. To independently validate their findings, the scientists examined brain scans from another 224 children participating in a separate research project called the Healthy Brain Network. Each child in this additional group had been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety disorder.

The team developed an artificial intelligence model to investigate functional connectivity, which describes how different regions of the brain work together. By incorporating diagnostic information and behavioral test results, the model identified patterns of brain connectivity that were more pronounced in children with ADHD, anxiety or both compared with those who had neither condition.

Combining behavioral information with brain imaging data revealed two major dimensions of dysfunction associated with ADHD and anxiety: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction.

Each dimension involves a different network of brain regions. Different combinations of these disruptions produced three distinct biotypes, which the researchers named the externalizing-disinhibited biotype, the internalizing-distressed biotype and the mixed biotype.

Three Distinct Brain Types and Their Symptoms

The three biological categories were mutually exclusive (each child was in only one biotype), but none was limited to a particular traditional diagnosis.

Children belonging to the externalizing-disinhibited group tended to exhibit higher levels of impulsivity, hostility, defiance, aggression and rule-breaking behavior. ADHD diagnoses were more common among children in this group.

The internalizing-distressed group was characterized by greater feelings of guilt and tension, stronger perfectionist tendencies, and more symptoms associated with anxiety and depression. Children with this biological profile were more frequently diagnosed with anxiety disorders.

Those in the mixed group experienced more difficulties with attention, irritability and self-injury. Like children in the externalizing-disinhibited group, they were more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis.

Despite these tendencies, researchers found every combination of brain biotype and conventional diagnosis among the children they studied.

Brain Changes Could Reveal ADHD and Anxiety Before Diagnosis

One of the most surprising findings emerged when scientists examined brain scans taken from children who had not been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety when they first entered the study.

The distinctive biological patterns were already detectable in their initial scans, even though the children did not receive a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both until later.

"We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions," Zhang said, noting that identifying these patterns before diagnosis was the most unexpected aspect of the research. "It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression."

Toward More Personalized ADHD and Anxiety Treatments

Zhang does not expect the newly identified brain biotypes to replace conventional diagnoses based on symptoms. Instead, combining the two approaches could help clinicians select treatments that are better suited to individual children.

Finding an effective treatment for ADHD or anxiety currently involves considerable experimentation. Children may need to try several medications before discovering which one provides meaningful relief.

"When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time -- a couple of weeks or months -- to see a response," Zhang said. "If the first medication doesn't work, they switch to a different one"

This process can be lengthy, expensive and frustrating.

Zhang hopes future clinical trials will build on the team's findings by investigating how different treatments affect specific patterns of brain activity. Such studies could eventually help researchers determine which therapies are most effective for each of the three biotypes.

"We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time," he said.

Researchers involved in the study are affiliated with Stanford University's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute and the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

Additional contributors came from the University of Iowa, the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01MH129694, R01MH136197, R01MH145082, R01MH140425, U24AA021697, R01DA057567, R37MH101495 and R01MH132784), the Eagles Autism Foundation, the Stanford Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience, the Rosenkranz Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Effie and Wofford Cain Foundation.

articles.personality_title: Stanford study finds three hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety in children
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and anxiety are common mental health problems in children. Doctors usually diagnose them by looking at symptoms, but these two conditions often share similar signs, making it hard to understand what’s really happening in the brain.

**What happened** – Scientists at Stanford used artificial intelligence (AI) to study thousands of brain scans from children with ADHD, anxiety, or both. They discovered three different brain types, called biotypes, which show unique patterns in how brain areas work together. These biotypes don’t match the usual diagnoses exactly but reveal hidden biological differences.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it could help doctors find ADHD and anxiety earlier, even before symptoms become clear. Knowing a child’s brain biotype might also help doctors choose treatments that work better for each child, instead of trying many medicines one by one. This could make treatment faster and more effective.

**What’s next step** – Researchers want to test how different treatments affect each brain biotype. They hope future studies will use these brain patterns to guide doctors in giving the right therapy at the right time, improving care for children with ADHD and anxiety.

**One-sentence takeaway** – AI has uncovered three hidden brain types in children with ADHD and anxiety, opening the door to earlier diagnosis and more personalized treatments.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
articles.summary: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.
articles.content:
A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer. Researchers at Rockefeller University have discovered that these immune molecules help regulate the growth of cells lining the intestine, potentially preventing the uncontrolled cell division that can lead to tumors.

In a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody. The researchers also uncovered how this protection works. IgA attaches to cells along the intestinal lining and helps prevent them from multiplying too rapidly.

Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer showed an elevated risk of developing tumors.

"One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer," says senior author Daniel Mucida, who leads Rockefeller's Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. "Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?"

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, a condition in which the body produces little or none of this antibody, face a greater risk of colorectal cancer. They also offer new insight into how gut bacteria, immune defenses, and intestinal cells work together to influence cancer development, potentially even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems.

Why the Gut Contains So Much of This Antibody

IgA is one of the immune system's most abundant antibodies in the digestive tract, where it provides an important early defense against potentially harmful microbes. Unlike antibodies that recognize a single specific target, IgA can interact with many different kinds of gut bacteria and even certain healthy cells belonging to the body.

Scientists have known for decades that the intestines contain unusually large quantities of IgA. However, the reasons for its abundance, and the full range of functions it performs, have remained incompletely understood.

Mucida's laboratory investigates how the intestine manages two essential but sometimes competing responsibilities. It must defend the body against dangerous microorganisms while allowing nutrients from food to pass into the bloodstream. Earlier research from his team has also helped explain how immune cells in the digestive tract contribute to food intolerances and allergies.

For the new study, Gregory Donaldson, a former postdoctoral researcher at Rockefeller who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, set out to better understand how IgA interacts with intestinal bacteria and whether those interactions might influence the development of colon cancer.

"We know these antibodies bind bacteria and, by doing so, can shape the microbiome," he says. "And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease."

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms living in and on the body. In the intestines, these microbes perform important functions related to digestion and immune health, but certain bacteria can also contribute to disease under the wrong conditions.

Missing Gut Antibodies More Than Doubled Colon Tumors

To investigate IgA's protective effects, Donaldson compared mice that could not produce the antibody with mice that had normal IgA levels. Both groups were raised together, allowing the researchers to control for differences in food and exposure to microorganisms.

The results revealed a striking difference. Animals without IgA developed substantially more colorectal tumors than their counterparts, consistent with the increased colorectal cancer risk observed in humans with IgA deficiency.

The association was not limited to a single experimental setup. Researchers observed the same pattern using multiple models of colon cancer, strengthening the evidence that IgA plays a meaningful protective role.

"We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect," says Donaldson.

The team then tested whether replacing the missing antibody could reverse the effect. When mice lacking IgA received oral doses of the antibody, their increased susceptibility to colon tumors disappeared.

This result suggested that IgA does more than simply accompany other protective processes in the intestine. Its presence appears to directly influence conditions that determine whether tumors develop.

Scientists Discover a Natural Brake on Cancer Cell Growth

To understand the mechanism behind this protection, the researchers examined epithelial cells, which form the inner lining of the intestine. These cells are particularly important because colon cancer begins when cells in this tissue undergo changes that allow them to grow uncontrollably.

The intestinal lining is constantly renewing itself. Older or damaged cells are replaced by new ones, making controlled cell division essential for keeping the digestive tract healthy. However, when the signals that regulate this process become disrupted, excessive growth can create opportunities for cancer to develop.

In mice without IgA, the researchers identified changes in gene activity associated with cell proliferation, the process through which cells divide and increase in number. Crucially, these changes appeared before any tumors became visible, suggesting that the antibody helps regulate an early step in cancer development.

"We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this," Donaldson says.

The researchers suspected that IgA was interacting with a specific molecular structure on the surface of intestinal cells, allowing it to influence how those cells behaved.

Gabriella Lima dos Reis, the study's second author and a graduate student working in Gabriel Victora's laboratory, investigated a promising candidate called DMBT1.

DMBT1 is a receptor found on the surface of epithelial cells that can bind to IgA. Previous research had connected it to several types of cancer, but scientists had not established precisely how it functions in the development of colon tumors.

How Gut Bacteria and IgA Control Tumor Formation

Further experiments revealed that DMBT1 plays two very different roles depending on whether IgA is present.

When intestinal bacteria are present, DMBT1 activates signals that encourage epithelial cells to divide. This response is part of the normal activity of the intestinal lining, which must continually replace cells to maintain its protective barrier.

IgA helps keep that growth under control. When the antibody binds to DMBT1, it restrains the receptor's activity, effectively acting as a brake on cell proliferation.

Without IgA, however, DMBT1 signaling can continue without sufficient restraint. Intestinal cells then divide more rapidly than they should, increasing the likelihood that tumors will develop.

The researchers confirmed that this excessive growth depends on several interacting factors. When gut bacteria were absent, DMBT1 signaling was disabled, or normal amounts of IgA were available, epithelial cell division remained under control.

Together, these findings reveal how a common immune molecule helps maintain the delicate balance between necessary tissue renewal and potentially dangerous overgrowth.

"If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function -- responding to bacteria by producing new cells -- can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer," Mucida says. "We think this homeostatic effect is IgA's main function. This was a big surprise."

Homeostasis refers to the body's ability to maintain stable, healthy conditions despite constant changes in its environment. In this case, IgA appears to support that balance by preventing normal intestinal cell renewal from becoming excessive.

A New Possibility for Preventing Colon Cancer

By identifying DMBT1's normal role in intestinal cells, the Rockefeller team has uncovered a potential target for future colon cancer prevention strategies.

Instead of waiting until a tumor develops and then attempting to destroy it, researchers may eventually be able to influence the biological signals that make tumors more likely to form.

"Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor," Mucida says. "We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point."

Colon polyps are growths that develop along the inner lining of the large intestine. Although many are harmless, some can eventually become cancerous. Removing them during a colonoscopy can reduce cancer risk, but researchers are interested in finding additional ways to prevent future tumors from developing.

The newly identified IgA and DMBT1 pathway could offer one such opportunity, although additional research is needed to determine whether targeting it would be effective and safe in humans.

Could Beneficial Gut Bacteria Help Prevent Cancer?

The discovery also raises another intriguing possibility. Certain intestinal bacteria may actively help protect against cancer by influencing how epithelial cells behave or by encouraging the production of protective antibodies.

While much of the research into the gut microbiome and cancer has focused on harmful bacteria that promote tumor formation or accelerate cancer growth, some microbes may have the opposite effect.

"What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well," Donaldson notes. "A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it's one direction that we could look towards in the future."

Such an approach would aim to use beneficial microorganisms to stimulate the body's existing protective mechanisms rather than directly attacking cancer cells. However, the idea remains speculative, and the mouse experiments do not establish that taking IgA supplements or probiotics can prevent colon cancer in people.

For now, the findings provide a clearer picture of how the immune system and gut microbiome cooperate to maintain healthy intestinal tissue. They also suggest that some of the body's most important defenses against cancer may operate long before the disease becomes detectable.

Mucida adds, "Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health."

articles.title: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03718-4Potent immune responses against diverse HIV strains have ignited the field, but major hurdles remain.
articles.content:
In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” says Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

Shots in the dark

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

One overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” says Burton.

Scouting for talented B cells

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Booster shots

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, says virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

articles.personality_title: Scientists edge closer to an effective HIV vaccine using powerful antibodies
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – HIV is a virus that has been difficult to fight because it changes quickly and has many versions. For decades, scientists have tried to create a vaccine but faced many challenges. A key discovery was a special kind of antibody found in some people living with HIV that can fight many types of the virus.

**What happened** – Researchers studied a woman from South Africa, known as CAP256, who made very strong antibodies against HIV. By understanding how her immune system worked, scientists developed new vaccine ideas that train the body to make similar powerful antibodies. Recent tests in monkeys and early human trials show these vaccines can create the right kind of immune response to block HIV.

**Impact** – This is important because these powerful antibodies, called broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), can stop many HIV strains. Previous vaccines could not do this. If successful, the vaccine could protect people before they get infected, which would be a big step forward in fighting HIV worldwide.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue testing these vaccines in more people to see if they can safely and effectively prevent HIV infections. They will also work on improving the vaccines to make them stronger and longer-lasting.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New vaccines inspired by rare but strong antibodies offer hope for a future HIV vaccine that can protect against many virus strains.

articles.title: Why a Viagra-like blood flow drug may open a new front against Alzheimer’s
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The post Why a Viagra-like blood flow drug may open a new front against Alzheimer’s first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance.

How the Alzheimer’s pill works

A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug

AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory,” she said.

That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function,” she said.

A tablet instead of an infusion

The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.”

Phase 3 trial results in detail

13 countries, 604 key participants

The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD, enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said.

The subgroup question

The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation.

Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment

Regulators and further trials

None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition.

A different route against dementia

The stakes are large. Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs.

articles.personality_title: New daily pill slows memory loss in early Alzheimer’s patients
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Alzheimer’s disease causes memory loss and thinking problems, affecting millions worldwide. Most current treatments target a protein called amyloid, but they often require injections and don’t fully stop the disease.

**What happened** – A new pill called AR1001, taken once a day, was tested in a large study across 13 countries. It slowed memory and thinking decline by 31% over one year in people with early Alzheimer’s who were not using other Alzheimer’s medicines. The pill works by improving blood flow to the brain, similar to how Viagra works for blood vessels.

**Impact** – This is important because AR1001 uses a different method than current drugs. Instead of targeting amyloid, it helps brain cells by increasing blood flow and supporting learning and memory pathways. Also, being a simple pill makes it easier for patients compared to treatments given by injection.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to run more studies to confirm these results and understand why the pill didn’t show the same benefit in patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs. The results must also be reviewed by health authorities before the pill can be prescribed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – AR1001, a new once-daily pill improving blood flow, shows promise in slowing memory loss for early Alzheimer’s patients not on other treatments, offering a fresh approach to the disease.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle pilule quotidienne ralentit la perte de mémoire chez les patients atteints d’Alzheimer précoce
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La maladie d’Alzheimer provoque des pertes de mémoire et des troubles de la réflexion, touchant des millions de personnes dans le monde. La plupart des traitements actuels ciblent une protéine appelée amyloïde, mais nécessitent souvent des injections et ne stoppent pas complètement la maladie.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une nouvelle pilule nommée AR1001, prise une fois par jour, a été testée dans une grande étude menée dans 13 pays. Elle a ralenti de 31 % la perte de mémoire et de réflexion sur un an chez des personnes atteintes d’Alzheimer précoce ne prenant pas d’autres médicaments contre la maladie. Cette pilule agit en améliorant le flux sanguin au cerveau, un peu comme le Viagra agit sur les vaisseaux sanguins.

**Impact** – C’est important car AR1001 utilise une méthode différente des médicaments actuels. Au lieu de cibler l’amyloïde, elle aide les cellules du cerveau en augmentant le flux sanguin et en soutenant les voies de l’apprentissage et de la mémoire. De plus, sous forme de pilule, elle est plus facile à prendre que les traitements injectables.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent réaliser d’autres études pour confirmer ces résultats et comprendre pourquoi la pilule n’a pas montré les mêmes bénéfices chez les patients déjà sous d’autres médicaments contre Alzheimer. Les résultats doivent aussi être examinés par les autorités sanitaires avant que la pilule puisse être prescrite.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – AR1001, une nouvelle pilule quotidienne améliorant le flux sanguin, montre un potentiel pour ralentir la perte de mémoire chez les patients atteints d’Alzheimer précoce ne suivant pas d’autres traitements, offrant une nouvelle voie contre la maladie.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva píldora diaria ralentiza la pérdida de memoria en pacientes con Alzheimer temprano
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La enfermedad de Alzheimer causa pérdida de memoria y problemas de pensamiento, afectando a millones en todo el mundo. La mayoría de los tratamientos actuales se enfocan en una proteína llamada amiloide, pero suelen requerir inyecciones y no detienen completamente la enfermedad.

**Qué pasó** – Una nueva píldora llamada AR1001, que se toma una vez al día, fue probada en un gran estudio en 13 países. Ralentizó la pérdida de memoria y pensamiento en un 31 % durante un año en personas con Alzheimer temprano que no usaban otros medicamentos para la enfermedad. La píldora funciona mejorando el flujo sanguíneo en el cerebro, similar a cómo el Viagra actúa en los vasos sanguíneos.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque AR1001 usa un método diferente a los medicamentos actuales. En lugar de atacar la amiloide, ayuda a las células cerebrales aumentando el flujo sanguíneo y apoyando los caminos del aprendizaje y la memoria. Además, al ser una píldora simple, es más fácil para los pacientes que los tratamientos con inyecciones.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren hacer más estudios para confirmar estos resultados y entender por qué la píldora no mostró el mismo beneficio en pacientes que ya tomaban otros medicamentos para Alzheimer. Los resultados también deben ser revisados por las autoridades sanitarias antes de que se pueda recetar la píldora.

**Frase clave** – AR1001, una nueva píldora diaria que mejora el flujo sanguíneo, muestra potencial para ralentizar la pérdida de memoria en pacientes con Alzheimer temprano que no usan otros tratamientos, ofreciendo un enfoque nuevo para la enfermedad.
